health.actionAddPhrasingHint: Adds the wording people actually type as a new row that sits alongside the original title and shares the same answer — it does not replace the original title. The original wording is often the real input, and changing it takes a phrasing people really do use out of the index. The new row copies every field of the original and only swaps the title, so tags, validity date and as-of date all come along.
health.actionDisableHint: Rewrites the validity date of these records to a sentinel date in the past so they leave the retrieval set. The data stays in the source file and in the index, its validity has simply passed; if the call was wrong, put that cell back and they return. This requires the tenant to have declared a date dimension with the valid_until role under “Tag dimensions” first, so that the data has somewhere to express “disabled” — without it this action is refused, and it says what is missing. Tick at least one; ticking them all disables every record this finding involves (all of them are ticked by default).
health.actionDismissHint: The only one of the five that touches no data: it records on this row who decided it is not a problem, when, and why. The reason is required — a blank reason means only half of it is on record and the next person has to make the call all over again. Once decided, this finding leaves the open list until the evidence or the confidence really changes.
health.actionMergeHint: Folds the phrasings of the other records into the top of the one you keep and disables the rest without deleting them. One document should carry every phrasing: deleting them all leaves the people who use those phrasings with nothing, while keeping them all eats several of the top sixteen retrieval slots. This action is not offered on QA sets — for direct answers extra phrasings are an asset, not a duplicate, and merging them into one disables the direct answers for those phrasings.
health.actionSupersedeHint: Writes “I have been superseded by this one” onto the superseded records so that recency convergence can follow the pointer to the current version. The value written is the external key of the file the current version lives in, so the granularity is the file: the current version and the superseded records cannot be in the same file, and the file holding the current version must have an external key, or the pointer leads nowhere. This action also requires the tenant to have declared a dimension with the superseded_by role first.
health.actionUndoHint: Rolls back what the last disposal did to the data and puts this finding back on the open list. Undo does not always succeed: it is only well defined while what the disposal wrote is untouched — if the data has been changed since, writing the old value back would wipe out that later change too, so the backend refuses and names the cell that no longer matches. Merge especially: once the same record has been merged a second time by another finding, that one line holds both rounds of phrasings and no single rewrite counts as the inverse. When it is refused, edit the data directly instead of using undo.
health.actionsHint: These are not “mark as read” — each one really changes your data; the single exception is “Not a problem”, which only writes this finding row. They disable or add, never delete; every one of them leaves an audit trail and every one of them can be undone. Which of them this finding offers is decided by the backend, and the page only draws the ones the backend offers.
health.crossDataset: Spans datasets, or belongs to none
health.disableReasonPlaceholder: Why these records should be disabled
health.dismissReasonPlaceholder: Why this is not a problem
health.findingsSortHint: This list is ordered by “check → finding id”, not by impact: retrieval hit counts live in the upstream conversation logs and cannot go into a database sort, and this list is paged — ordering within one page is a fake ordering, and the record on page 2 that is retrieved 50 times a day would never reach page 1. To read by impact, use the overview above.
health.hitChecks: The three that need conversation logs:
health.hitChecksLegend: ran = they were computed this time; not_requested = they were not asked for this time (the stale-but-often-retrieved, never-retrieved and often-asked-never-answered lists keep the previous result, which is not the same as “no problems”); unavailable = they were asked for but the conversation logs could not be fetched, reason on the next line.
health.includeHitChecks: Also recompute the three that need conversation logs (stale but often retrieved / never retrieved / often asked, never answered)
health.includeHitChecksHint: Those three can only be computed by fetching a whole time window of conversation logs from upstream, so they are off by default: when you re-check right after a disposal what changed is the data, and hit statistics do not move within a second. Leaving it on just pays for one upstream fetch per click, and ties “can I re-check” to “is the statistics upstream alive”. The daily full rescan always computes them.
health.intro: The health check pulls out the data that answers, but answers wrongly: duplicated phrasings, numbers that contradict each other, expired answers that are still being retrieved. The check itself only reads — it will not change a single character of your data. What changes data is the disposal actions below, and every one of them leaves an audit trail and can be undone.
health.lastScanNever: This tenant has not run a health check yet. Press “Re-check” above to run the first one; the system also runs one right after data is imported. Until then the overview and the list below are empty — which means “not checked yet”, not “checked and clean”.
health.overviewDaysRangeSuffix: days. Changing this cell recomputes the window above and the whole table.
health.overviewSortHint: This table is not ordered by how many findings there are. It is ordered by the total number of times the records in each group were retrieved during the time window — one duplicate that has never been retrieved matters far less than one expired answer that is retrieved 50 times a day. Replays from batch regression runs are already excluded from the hit counts, so running a regression will not push the replayed records to the top.
health.overviewTopHintPrefix: Each group lists only its top
health.overviewTopHintSuffix: , and that is not paging: its purpose is to bring the ones worth looking at first in front of you. When a group has more open findings than that, the rest are only visible in the list below.
health.overviewTopNField: How many to list per group
health.overviewTopNRangeSuffix: records. This is the cap on how many the “worth looking at first” column lists, not paging; the rest are only visible in the list below.
health.overviewWindowHintMid: days rather than 30 by default: upstream aggregates at most
health.overviewWindowHintSuffix: conversations per request, and for a moderately busy tenant a 30-day window is bound to cross that line, which would make the overview impossible to open. When a longer window cannot be opened, the response says that is the reason.
health.partialHint: The numbers below say which records had which check skipped — they do not say “checked and clean”. On the findings list those two look identical: the list can only show findings that were computed, never “this check was not run at all”.
health.recordSourceHint: The marker in front of a title says what that title is, and the three are not the same kind of thing: [Row] = the title cell of a row-wise import (merging writes exactly that string into the source file); [Whole document] = one file imported from a folder, where the title is its original filename, not its content; [What people asked] = a group of questions that got no answer, which was never a record in the knowledge base to begin with. The id after it is the value the disposal actions actually send.
health.recordTitleBlank: (the title cell of this record is empty)
health.recordUnavailable: (the title of this record cannot be read)
health.reopenedHint: A disposed finding only comes back to the list when the premise of the original decision changed — that is, the evidence computed this time, or the confidence, is not the same as when the decision was made. If the premise has not changed, re-checking only updates “Last seen” and does not push it back. An undone disposal also lands here. Below is the reason the system wrote down, including the evidence as it stood at the time of the disposal.
health.reopenedTitle: This one was disposed of, and came back to the open list
health.scanExactMatchOnly: Records too long to compare, matched only character for character:
health.scanExactMatchOnlyHint: For records over the length limit, the near-duplicate check only decided whether they are character-for-character identical this time: the same document uploaded twice is still caught, but “almost the same two documents” was not compared. The limit exists because similarity is a pairwise comparison — a single pair of long documents takes tens of seconds, and a few dozen monthly reports sharing one template would make the whole scan never finish, which stops every check at once and is worse than one check under-reporting.
health.scanFailedHint: That attempt failed, so the numbers below are still from the last check that succeeded, not from the most recent one. A failure never overwrites the last successful result — overwriting it would take “which files were not looked at that time” away as well. This block disappears after the next successful check.
health.scanFailedTitle: The most recent check did not finish
health.scanRecordLimitHint: When “Records read” goes over the per-run limit, nothing is checked and no finding is written at all: near-duplicate detection compares every pair, and past the limit the check would run longer than anyone waits — while “scanned half of it” and “scanned all of it” look exactly the same on the list. The limit after the slash is given by the backend; it is not a number written into the page.
health.scanSlotless: Records with no field slots, where the two tag checks do not apply:
health.scanSlotlessHint: A whole document imported from a folder has no field slots — column mapping only exists for row-wise imports, and there is no path that could write tags onto them. So the tag-gap and missing-as-of checks exclude them: these records will not show up on the list for being untagged, and that does not mean they are tagged. To bring this content under dimension filtering, import it row by row instead.
health.scanTooShort: Records too short, skipped for near-duplicate comparison:
health.scanTooShortHint: Records whose content is too short never enter near-duplicate grouping at all: similarity always scores a perfect match for two identical pieces of text, and the boilerplate answers a Q&A set is full of (“none”, “yes”, “not applicable”, “as above”) are only a few characters long — without a lower bound they would all collapse into one finding carrying thousands of records, burying the real near-duplicates behind it. The cost is that genuine repetition among those few is not reported either — two answers that both say “none” were never duplicates to begin with (the repetition is in the questions, which is a different check; an answer with no substance is the “no real content” check).
health.scanTriggerLegend: manual = somebody pressed “Re-check” above; import = the run that follows a data import; daily = the scheduled full rescan (only that one always computes the three checks that need conversation logs). “The last check was 20 minutes ago” does not mean the same thing when somebody just pressed the button as when the scheduler ran it.
health.supersedeCurrent: Which one is the current version
health.supersedeRestHint: The records not chosen as the current version are the ones it supersedes.
health.uncoveredCount: Listed in this table / not looked at in total:
health.uncoveredCountHint: When the two sides of the slash differ, the table below has been truncated: the first number is how many rows this table can show, the second is how many files were not looked at this time. The per-reason counts beside it are computed over all of them and are not affected by the truncation — for the group that got cut, that number is the only thing left to see.
health.uncoveredHint: These files are not part of this check — their content will not show up in any of the checks. They are listed because a missed problem is worse than a false one: a file nobody has looked at looks exactly like “clean” on the list.
health.uncoveredNone: Every file was looked at this time
health.uncoveredTitle: Files not looked at this time

help.dataImport.importOptions.title: About import options
help.dataImport.importOptions.what: This section decides how this import gets written into the dataset, applying to every field mapping you just set up: whether to convert any leftover HTML in the content into clean Markdown, and whether to use the same external key to replace previously imported data with this new version — the way to avoid piling up duplicate old data every time the same file gets re-imported.
help.dataImport.pdfBatchImportResult.wha: This section lists the outcome of this batch of PDF/WORD documents file by file: each file is marked as succeeded or failed, failed files show a reason, and successes and failures are shown side by side — a few failed files never hide the results for the rest of the batch. The last column is a different thing: whether that file made it into the search index, again marked per file. A file whose import itself failed has no indexing job to look up, so that cell reads “No indexing job”.
help.dataset.chunkSettings.title: About chunking settings
help.dataset.chunkSettings.what: This section decides how files imported into this dataset get split into chunks afterwards: how big each chunk is, whether adjacent chunks keep an overlapping stretch of text so a sentence doesn’t get cut in half, and whether each chunk carries the source document’s title so retrieval can tell which document a passage came from.
help.demo.maxAnswerCharsEffect: Truncated from the end, with “Content too long — showing only the first N characters” appended
help.demo.maxSourcesEffect: Only the highest-scoring sources up to the cap are shown; the rest are omitted
help.demo.title: Answer length limit
help.demo.what: This section controls how many characters a single answer can output; anything past the limit is truncated and does not affect how many sources were retrieved.
help.extractKey.currentKey.title: About the current key
help.extractKey.currentKey.what: This section manages this tenant’s extraction API key: whether one exists, the full plaintext right when it’s generated (shown only that once — after that the system keeps only a hash and a short hint of it), and regenerating a new key. This key is a tenant-level credential for external programs to call the extraction API and the data API via the X-API-Key header; it does not constitute any user’s login identity. Regenerating invalidates the old key immediately, so make sure the new key is deployed everywhere it’s called before doing it.
help.extractKey.howToTitle.textEffect: Out of range returns 400 and names the offending field; it is not truncated and sent anyway.
help.extractKey.howToTitle.timeRefEffect: Same as above; this field, like text, goes verbatim into the prompt, so it is bounded too.
help.extractKey.howToTitle.title: About calling the extraction API
help.extractKey.howToTitle.what: This section demonstrates how to call the extraction API: which header to send, which fields the request needs, and a curl example you can copy and run directly. This is documentation, not something that sends a request itself — it shows how to use the key above, not a separate credential to manage on its own.
help.health.findings.title: About the findings list
help.health.findings.what: This section is the finding-by-finding list, filterable by disposal status and check type, and the only place dispositive actions are actually taken — by default it only shows undisposed findings, a to-do list rather than a full history; switch disposal status to “resolved” or “all” to see ones already judged.
help.health.lastScan.title: About the last scan
help.health.lastScan.what: This section shows the result of the most recent successful scan as stored, not the live response from this operation — the scan result is persisted, so refreshing the page, or even signing in from a different device, still shows which files weren’t seen last time and whether each check ran, without needing to be watching the screen the moment rescan was clicked.
help.health.overview.title: About the impact-ranked overview
help.health.overview.what: This section groups open findings by check type and sums up their impact, with each group’s highest-priority few attached — it answers which check type matters most overall for this tenant right now, not a browsable list; taking action on an individual finding still happens in the findings list below.
help.health.partial.title: About checks not completed this time
help.health.partial.what: This section counts records that some checks structurally don’t apply to this time — not “checked and found fine”: whole documents from folder imports have no field slots, so tag-gap and missing-as-of-date can’t measure them; records whose content is longer than the pairwise comparison limit only get an exact-match check from near-duplicate this time, not the “almost identical” kind; and records whose content is too short never enter grouping at all — that is what keeps boilerplate answers like “none”, “yes” and “not applicable” from collapsing into one fake duplicate group of thousands, at the cost of not reporting genuine repetition among them.
help.health.rescan.title: About rescanning now
help.health.rescan.what: This section triggers a fresh scan of this tenant: every piece of data gets run through whichever checks apply this time (the “also recompute” checkbox below decides whether to include the checks that need Q&A history — the rest always run), and whatever findings come out get written into the list below — the check itself only reads, never writes, so it never touches your data. “Scan scope” only decides which findings get merged back into the list this time (for example, re-verifying a single dataset right after disposing of it); the comparison itself always runs against the whole tenant’s data, so cross-dataset findings never get missed.
help.health.uncovered.title: About files not seen this time
help.health.uncovered.what: This section lists files whose content this scan never read at all — not scanned and found clean, but never looked at by any check, whether because the format has no local extractor, the original file is missing from disk, the extractor failed to read it, or the file wasn’t row-imported so its per-row document id can’t be computed.
help.limitsTitle: All the numbers for this section
help.qaSet.addQaSet.title: About adding a QA set
help.qaSet.addQaSet.what: This section creates a new QA set. It shares the same creation mechanism as a regular dataset, so it also needs a group assigned — who can later import into, edit, or delete this QA set depends on who has data-write permission for that group, the same rule as file-type datasets.
help.qaSet.qaSetList.title: About the QA set list
help.qaSet.qaSetList.what: This section lists every QA set, where you can import Q&A pairs or delete a set. Deleting a QA set also removes it from every conversation setting that referenced it, so no setting is left pointing at a deleted QA set; if a conversation setting itself has an invalid field, the deletion is blocked with a prompt to fix it on the conversation settings page instead of a vague “deletion failed”.
help.regression.addCase.title: About adding a case manually
help.regression.addCase.what: This section manually enters a case: a question, optional preceding turns for testing follow-up scenarios, and at least one assertion. An assertion states a condition the answer must satisfy — for example, must contain a given string, must cite a given document, or must honestly answer “not found” — and at least one of them must be deterministic, because a case scored only by subjective judging always passes and can never detect a regression.
help.regression.addSuite.title: About adding a suite
help.regression.addSuite.what: This section creates a new suite: a container that later holds cases you replay over and over to check for regressions. Its name is how you identify it — every case you add and every execution recorded afterward belongs to this suite.
help.regression.bucketJudgeDrift.title: About judge drift
help.regression.bucketJudgeDrift.what: This section lists cases whose deterministic verdict did not change, but whose subjective scores went from scored to entirely unscored this run — or the other way around. Whether these cases pass or fail truly did not change; only the judge itself broke or recovered this time, which is a different question from whether the answer regressed, so it is called out separately instead of being buried inside “Unchanged” where it would look like subjective scoring kept working as usual.
help.regression.bucketNotCompared.title: About not compared
help.regression.bucketNotCompared.what: This section lists cases where only one of the two runs has a result — the case may have been added after the baseline ran, or either run may have been aborted before reaching it. Whether these cases regressed simply was not measured this time, so they are deliberately excluded from “Unchanged” — otherwise a run that aborted partway through would misleadingly read as “nothing changed”.
help.regression.bucketRegressed.title: About regressed
help.regression.bucketRegressed.what: This section lists cases that both runs have a result for, where the verdict changed from passing to failing — this is the entire reason the regression report exists, catching which previously correct answers this change (a new model, a tweaked prompt, a changed retrieval setting) broke. Classification looks only at deterministic assertions; a higher or lower subjective score never moves a case in or out of this list.
help.regression.casesOf.title: About the case list
help.regression.casesOf.what: This section expands the currently selected suite, listing each case’s question, number of preceding turns, and assertion count; the most common way to add a case is “Create case from a Q&A record”, which pulls in a real Q&A along with the expectations it can derive — manual entry has its own section below.
help.regression.compareSection.title: About comparing with a baseline
help.regression.compareSection.what: This section picks another execution of the same suite as a baseline and compares the two runs’ deterministic verdicts: regressions — cases that passed before and fail now — are the single most important signal in this report, and the documents each run cited are shown side by side so you can tell whether a change in retrieval results is what caused the regression. No comparison is shown below until a baseline is picked.
help.regression.effectiveSection.title: About what this run actually used
help.regression.effectiveSection.what: This section lists the settings actually sent to the answering engine for this run, recorded the moment it started and never affected by later changes to the profile; each row also marks whether that knob was deliberately set for this run or simply carried over from the profile under test, and once a baseline run is picked, its value is shown side by side along with whether the two differ.
help.regression.exportSection.title: About export
help.regression.exportSection.what: This section exports this run’s results as a CSV, in the column format the business team already uses for its Q&A report; if the run is still in progress or was aborted partway through, the exported file only contains the cases that finished, with its last row stating the actual row count and the abort reason so it is never misread as the whole suite having run.
help.regression.limitsSection.title: About this run’s limits
help.regression.limitsSection.what: This section lists the limits applied to this run, plus any truncation caused by the upstream conversation memory window: when a case’s preceding turns plus its own question exceed how many turns the upstream engine can remember at once, the earliest of those turns never reach the model, and this section names which cases are affected.
help.regression.perCase.title: About per-case results
help.regression.perCase.what: This section expands the full result of every case in this run: the actual answer, whether it passed, the measured value behind each failed assertion, the subjective score (or why there is none), which documents it cited, and how many preceding turns were actually sent. A low subjective score never fails a case — only a case with a judging criterion that the judge failed to score at all gets marked “judging incomplete”.
help.regression.runIdentity.title: About the run identity
help.regression.runIdentity.what: This section shows this execution’s identity and overall status: which suite it ran, which knowledge-retrieval profile and config version it used, and when it started and ended; if the run was aborted partway through, the abort reason is shown here, and while the cases that finished before the abort are kept, this is not a complete regression run.
help.regression.runList.title: About the execution history
help.regression.runList.what: This section lists every past execution of this suite, whether still running, finished, or aborted partway through; each row links to the full report or lets you download that run’s result CSV directly — an aborted run’s export only contains the cases that finished before it stopped.
help.regression.runSection.title: About running this suite
help.regression.runSection.what: This section runs this suite once against the selected knowledge-retrieval profile: by default every knob simply follows the profile under test’s current behavior, and only knobs where “Use a specified value this time” is checked get overridden — for this run only, never written back to the live profile. Every turn, including preceding turns, is a real question sent to the engine and consumes Q&A quota.
help.regression.suiteList.title: About the suite list
help.regression.suiteList.what: This section lists this tenant’s suites with each one’s case count and execution count; you can open a suite to see its cases, or delete a suite that has no execution history yet — a suite that already has execution history is kept, so a past run’s recorded totals never fall out of sync with the suite it was run against.
help.regression.summary.title: About the execution summary
help.regression.summary.what: This section summarizes this run’s overall results: how many cases finished, how many passed versus failed, the average subjective score, and how many preceding turns were sent in total. The average score only counts cases the judge actually scored — a case the judge failed to evaluate is never treated as a 0 that drags the average down.
help.serviceKey.issueTitle.title: About issuing a new credential
help.serviceKey.issueTitle.what: This section issues a new platform machine credential: enter a purpose name and one authorization scope and submit — the plaintext is shown exactly this once, right when issuing completes, and the system only keeps a hash of it afterward. This is a credential for callers that are not a person (for example, a scheduled job); it does not constitute anyone’s login identity. Only a platform system admin can issue one here; an auditor can see this page but cannot submit this action.
help.serviceKey.listTitle.title: About the existing credentials
help.serviceKey.listTitle.what: This section inventories every machine credential on the platform: name, authorization scope, hint of the tail, and issued / last-used / revoked times — this table can never surface the plaintext, because the system itself doesn’t retain it either. Auditors can read the whole table; only a platform system admin can revoke a credential here, and revocation is an immediate, soft delete — a revoked credential is never reactivated. The same scope can have multiple valid credentials at once, letting old and new coexist during a rotation.
help.serviceKey.plainTitle.title: About the just-issued plaintext key
help.serviceKey.plainTitle.what: This section shows the plaintext of the credential that was just issued and hasn’t been dismissed yet — the one and only place it ever appears in plaintext. Once this block is dismissed or the page is left, the system keeps only a hash and a short hint of it, and nobody can read the full plaintext back afterward. The copy button here is meant for pasting it into Secret Manager, not for leaving it in a terminal or a screen recording.
help.serviceKey.scopesTitle.title: About the authorization scopes that can be issued
help.serviceKey.scopesTitle.what: This section lists the authorization scopes the platform can currently issue, spelling out which endpoints each one covers — this list is itself the data source behind the scope dropdown in issuing, not a separate copy kept on this page. A scope decides what a credential can do: matching is exact-string both when issuing and when calling, so a value outside this list, or any endpoint outside the chosen scope, is always rejected. Auditors can read this section too.
help.settings.addAliasTable.title: About adding an alias table
help.settings.addAliasTable.what: This section creates a new alias table, registering a set of phrasings a user might use (abbreviations, colloquial wording) as the same thing — one canonical form plus its aliases — so matching can map the user’s wording back to the same term or record.
help.settings.addGlossaryTable.title: About adding a glossary table
help.settings.addGlossaryTable.what: This section creates a new glossary table. Each table generates its own query tool that the agent can call in agent mode, letting it look up the terms defined here whenever it needs to. The query normalization regex decides what to strip from a user’s input (for example, differences in punctuation or whitespace) before matching it against the table’s entries; leave it blank and only basic normalization applies.
help.settings.addGroup.title: About adding a group
help.settings.addGroup.what: This section creates a new group: enter a group name and tick which fine-grained capabilities to grant it (data and settings each split into read/write; ask, history, and audit are each a single toggle). A group holds no members by itself — after creating it, go to the Member Management page to assign members into it; a member’s capabilities are the union of every group it belongs to.
help.settings.addMcpServer.title: About adding an MCP Server
help.settings.addMcpServer.what: This section registers a new MCP Server: enter its name, command, and the rest of its definition and submit, and it’s added to the single registry shared across the whole platform — it doesn’t belong to any one tenant. Because registering one means executing the command you enter on the agent host, only a platform system administrator can create one here; each tenant can only check off already-registered servers on its own conversation settings page.
help.settings.addMember.passwordEffect: Below the minimum it is rejected in this field, not after submission; there is no maximum.
help.settings.addMember.title: About adding a member
help.settings.addMember.what: This section creates a new tenant member: submitted together with a login email, initial password, which groups it belongs to (multi-select), and whether it is a tenant admin. What this member can actually do afterward comes from the union of capabilities across every group it belongs to — it is not ticked item by item here; checking “tenant admin” bypasses that group limit entirely, granting every capability in this tenant plus the ability to manage other members and groups. What gets set here is a tenant-internal role, a different thing from a platform system admin’s cross-tenant identity.
help.settings.addSkill.title: About adding a Skill
help.settings.addSkill.what: This section creates a new Skill: enter a name and a purpose description and submit, and GufoRAG chatbot builds a new instructions-plus-tool-whitelist definition; the purpose description is what the agent uses to decide when to call it on its own, while the actual instructions, tool whitelist, and max iteration count are set afterwards in the editor.
help.settings.addTagDimension.title: About adding a tag dimension
help.settings.addTagDimension.what: This section declares a specific filterable field as a named, meaningful business dimension, which is what lets the controlled vocabulary section below define its valid values and lets intent classification recognize it and build retrieval filter conditions; a field that hasn’t been registered here is completely invisible to retrieval filtering.
help.settings.advancedPrompts.title: About advanced prompts
help.settings.advancedPrompts.what: This section holds the bot persona plus several additional system-prompt layers: bot role, Agent system prompt, respond prompt, intent-detection prompt, and chatroom prompt. Each layer maps to a different stage of the conversation flow, and is only sent to the model in whichever conversation mode actually has that stage.
help.settings.aliasTableList.title: About the alias table list
help.settings.aliasTableList.what: This section lists every alias table, where you can edit the name and description in place. Before a table can be deleted, if any conversation setting can still see it — whether it’s actually applied or just listed among that setting’s selectable alias tables — the system blocks the deletion and asks you to remove it from every field in conversation settings first, so no setting is left pointing at a table that no longer exists.
help.settings.answerability.title: About the answerability gate
help.settings.answerability.what: This section decides what happens when the collected or retrieved material is not enough to answer: with the gate on, a grounding decision runs first, and when the material is judged insufficient the reply honestly says so instead of letting the model fabricate an ungrounded answer. With the gate off that decision is skipped and the model generates a reply as usual.
help.settings.builtinTools.title: About built-in tools
help.settings.builtinTools.what: This section uses a per-tool three-state switch to control which built-in tools can be called in Agent conversation mode: all on = all enabled, some on = a whitelist, all off = every built-in tool disabled. Each card also lets you override the description shown to the model for that tool and append extra tool-level prompt text — both are written verbatim into the tool’s description, not engine parameters. This whole section is only used in Agent conversation mode.
help.settings.changePassword.title: About changing your password
help.settings.changePassword.what: This section changes only this account’s own login password, a separate action from the profile section above: on success, this account’s existing sessions on every other device are invalidated and must sign back in with the new password (the tab you used to change it stays signed in). This one deliberately ignores whether the tenant’s subscription period is active — the password can still be changed even after it has expired or before it has started, so the account is never locked out of fixing itself.
help.settings.generationParams.title: About generation parameters
help.settings.generationParams.what: This section controls how the main answer itself is generated: which model and reasoning depth to use, temperature, how much material to pull from the knowledge base, the topic-to-vector source ratio, the knowledge usage mode, and whether to rerank, plus conversation memory turns, response format, and time zone. These values are all sent by “Save conversation settings” at the bottom of the page; which model each internal LLM call other than the main answer uses is set in “Per-group LLM (advanced)” below.
help.settings.glossaryTableList.title: About the glossary table list
help.settings.glossaryTableList.what: This section lists every glossary table: you can edit the name, when-to-consult text, and supplementary instructions in place, or go in to manage its entries. Before a table can be deleted, if it’s still being used as a query tool by any skill or conversation setting, the system blocks the deletion and asks you to remove the reference first, so an in-use query tool doesn’t get deleted out from under it.
help.settings.groupList.title: About the group list
help.settings.groupList.what: This section lists every group in this tenant: you can edit a group’s name and capabilities in place, see how many members currently belong to it, open “Manage members” to add or remove users from it, or delete a group. A group that still has datasets assigned to it cannot be deleted — those datasets need to be moved to another group or reassigned first.
help.settings.mcpServerList.title: About the MCP Server list
help.settings.mcpServerList.what: This section lists every MCP Server currently registered platform-wide — one shared list across all tenants, not held separately per tenant — where you can edit connection settings in place, test the connection, see its most recent result, or delete a server that’s no longer in use.
help.settings.memberList.title: About the member list
help.settings.memberList.what: This section lists every member currently in this tenant: you can toggle each one’s active status, tenant-admin flag, and group membership (multi-select) in place — the effective-capabilities column is read-only, derived from the union of that member’s groups, and cannot be ticked directly here — and you can reset a member’s password. The system blocks any change that would leave the tenant with zero active admins; a platform system admin or auditor account that happens to live in this tenant cannot be altered here at all — those changes only happen on the platform admin side.
help.settings.myProfile.title: About my profile
help.settings.myProfile.what: This section holds the login user’s own display name and contact info, tied to this individual account. What sits in the account block above is tenant-level and a different matter: the quota and storage limit are read-only (only a platform admin can change them), while the company/unit is tenant-level too — changing it changes what everyone in this tenant sees — but anyone with the “settings” write capability can edit it. Saving here requires the tenant’s subscription period to currently be active; when it isn’t, these two fields are still visible but the save action is blocked.
help.settings.outputPipelineOrder.title: About the output pipeline order
help.settings.outputPipelineOrder.what: This section shows the fixed execution order of the three output post-processing stages: output replacement → output rules → compliance gate, with no entry point to reorder them. Because the compliance gate always runs last, text already rewritten by output replacement and output rules still gets checked by it.
help.settings.outputReplacements.title: About output replacement rules
help.settings.outputReplacements.what: This section defines deterministic text-replacement rules applied after the answer is generated: a hit on any alias in a rule is replaced with the same replacement content, using ${0} for the whole matched text or a named regex group ${name} to build things like links or formatted text. This step never touches the model — it’s plain-text post-processing that runs after the answer is generated (see “Output pipeline order” below for where it sits).
help.settings.policyTopics.title: About policy topics
help.settings.policyTopics.what: This section defines sensitive topics one row at a time: each topic has a name, definition, and examples, and lets you set independently, for both input and output, whether a hit should be blocked, recorded, or ignored. When blocked, it replies with that topic’s own refusal message; if left blank, it falls back to the input/output global blocked message below.
help.settings.qaDirectDecision.title: About direct-answer decisions
help.settings.qaDirectDecision.what: This section decides whether QA direct answer is on and which decision method it uses: off, exact match (the question must match the QA’s question after normalization), or exact match plus one LLM adjudication. On a hit the QA’s answer is returned verbatim without the model rephrasing it, so the knobs on the “Generation settings” tab do not apply to that reply.
help.settings.reasoningGroupsHeading.wha: This section lets you pick a model and reasoning depth for each of the five internal LLM calls other than the main answer — intent detection, judging (answerability / QA / policy), the tool loop, the skill subgraph, and suggested questions / chatroom topic — instead of inheriting the main answer’s settings for all of them. Leaving a group blank falls back to the main model with minimal reasoning (the existing default).
help.settings.skillList.title: About the Skill list
help.settings.skillList.what: This section lists every Skill this tenant currently has, showing each one’s purpose description, its currently active version, a rollup of the tools it can use, and whether it’s enabled; each row also has entry points to edit, try it out, enable/disable it, or delete it.
help.settings.systemPrompt.title: About the system prompt
help.settings.systemPrompt.what: This section edits this configuration’s system prompt (product_system_prompt), which is merged into the system prompt sent to the model on every turn and applies in both conversation modes. Every save creates a new version instead of overwriting the old one; the version list below lets you search, copy, or restore any past version.
help.settings.tagCoverageScan.title: About the tag coverage measurement scope
help.settings.tagCoverageScan.what: This section reads document content file by file to calculate how tagged each dimension is; the larger the measurement scope, the more documents it has to read. Tenants with a lot of data may exceed the per-scan limit, in which case narrowing “measurement scope” to a single dataset before re-measuring can help.
help.settings.tagDimensionList.title: About the tag dimension list
help.settings.tagDimensionList.what: This section lists every tag dimension: the coverage bar shows how much of the current scan scope has been tagged for that dimension, and for any dimension that isn’t fully tagged you can click “View untagged” to see exactly which documents are missing it, instead of hunting through datasets yourself. Date-type dimensions have no codes, so their row shows no code count and no “Edit vocabulary” action.
help.settings.tagFilter.title: About tag-based retrieval filtering
help.settings.tagFilter.what: This section holds an independent tag-retrieval-filter switch and time window for each configuration profile — they don’t affect each other, and you can turn on just one. Before it turns on, the system checks whether every file has the dimension fields it needs written into the index; whichever files are blocking it, and what to do about them, are listed in the table below.
help.settings.tagVocabulary.title: About controlled vocabulary (dictionary)
help.settings.tagVocabulary.what: This section edits the vocabulary for whichever dimension is currently selected in the tag dimension list above; to edit a different dimension, go back to that list and click “Edit vocabulary” on its row. Before a code can be deleted, if any conversation setting already has tag-based retrieval filtering turned on, the system blocks the deletion — once the code is gone, documents tagged with it would stop matching any filter condition on every future question, so filtering has to be turned off first.
help.widget.createToken.title: About generating a key
help.widget.createToken.what: This section generates an embed key: enter the domains it should be bound to and submit, and you get something to build the front-end embed link from. This key is for the tenant’s own public bot on its own website — it’s meant to be loaded by a browser, so anyone who views that page’s source can see it. Its protection isn’t secrecy; it’s that every call checks whether the calling origin is on the allow-list — a domain not on that list can’t make the key work even with a copy of it.
help.widget.tokenList.title: About the key list
help.widget.tokenList.what: This section lists every embed key currently in this tenant: name, the full key value, the domains it’s bound to, and its current status — each row can copy the full front-end embed link, or revoke a key that’s still active. The full key value is shown here as a matter of course, not just once, because it’s meant to already be sitting on the tenant’s own webpage — it isn’t a secret to hide. Revocation is irreversible: once revoked, every embedded page carrying that key stops working immediately.

platform.licenseUsageDesc: This is the daily Q&A cap that the GufoRAG license sells to the platform as a whole. It is not per tenant, and it is not any single tenant’s quota. “Today” is bounded by the platform timezone above.
platform.modelsAllOffHint: Once “No restriction” is unticked, this tenant can only use the models ticked below; ticking none means this tenant cannot use any model at all, which is not the same as no restriction.
platform.modelsUnrestricted: No restriction (this tenant may use every model)
platform.reviewDesc: Set the overdue threshold and list all matching accounts in one click; process them in a batch after confirmation. Fully manual; both the list and result screens persist for audit screenshots.
platform.reviewDueTooltip: Overdue for review; please review and act
platform.thresholdHint: The two thresholds are mutually exclusive: pick “Cut-off date” and that date wins — the overdue-days value has no effect (upstream reads only one of them, never both).
platform.thresholdMode: How the overdue threshold is computed (pick one)
platform.tracingCostHint: Once enabled, every question this tenant asks — along with the retrieved source text and the full answer — is stored in Langfuse. Existing conversations are unaffected; recording starts with new conversations.
platform.tracingEnable: Enable Langfuse tracing for this tenant
platform.trialOneOfHint: Extension days and a fixed expiry date are mutually exclusive: filling in both, or leaving both blank, is rejected on submit.

qa.exportRangeLimitPrefix: The download range spans at most

qa.exportWithHeaderHint: The stats header can only be produced by Summary (CSV); choosing Full detail drops this section. With this on, the first CSV row is no longer the column names — existing downstream parsers will misalign
qa.qaRecordIntro: This is the default landing page after signing in: a read-only preview of the conversation screen that front-end users actually see, where the “Q&A records” tab on the right lets you switch between sample conversations and “View sources” on a message shows which documents that answer cited along with the user’s satisfaction rating at the time. There’s no input box here and no way to send a new question — that only happens on the actual front-end page.
qaSet.intro: A QA set is a collection of question-answer pairs: when a question exactly matches an entry’s question, its answer is returned verbatim without AI rephrasing. Choose which QA sets take part in direct answering under Conversation Settings ▸ QA direct answer.
qaSet.previewFailed: Failed to read Excel columns; please check the file format
regression.abortedMeaning: This is not a complete regression run: only the cases listed below were actually replayed; for the rest, whether they regressed simply was not measured this time.
regression.addCaseIntro: Try “Create case from a Q&A record” first — assertions derived from a real record are more reliable than hand-written ones. Manual creation is for questions that have not been asked yet.
regression.aiTurnNotSent: On replay only the user half of each preceding turn is sent: the AI half is regenerated upstream (GufoRAG continues a conversation by chatroom id only — there is no field that can inject earlier AI replies).
regression.assertionCodeHint: One assertion carries exactly one code, and it must match the code in that dimension’s vocabulary verbatim, including case — the matcher cannot tell cases apart, so a wrong spelling simply never matches and reports no error. To require two codes, write two assertions.
regression.assertionCriteriaHint: The criteria text enters the prompt on every evaluation (one regression run is dozens of answers × several criteria each). Criteria length limit:
regression.assertionGate: At least one deterministic assertion is required. A subjective score never affects pass/fail — a case with only subjective scoring always passes and always lands in “Unchanged” in the baseline comparison, which means it can never detect a regression.
regression.assertionIdentityHint: Pick one. `document_id` is stable addressing — renaming the file will not turn the case red for no reason.
regression.assertionPatternHint: Only rules from the platform list — hand-written regular expressions are not accepted, because that would store an arbitrary pattern in the case and run it on the server on every execution.
regression.assertionPrefixHint: Leave empty to only require “has a link”. Do not type an empty string as “no prefix restriction” — every URL matches an empty prefix, so the assertion degrades into “is there a link” while you believe you restricted the domain.
regression.bucketFixedWhy: These failed in the baseline run and pass now.
regression.bucketJudgeDrift: Judge drift (subjective scores can no longer be measured)
regression.bucketJudgeDriftWhy: The deterministic verdicts of these cases really did not change, so they genuinely belong in “Unchanged” — but this run lost their subjective scores entirely. Without this block the report would read “nothing changed” while in fact this batch has no subjective score at all. It tracks the transition between “scored” and “not scored”, not how high the score is.
regression.bucketListedSuffix: are listed here — the number on the badge is the bucket total, not the row count of this table.
regression.bucketNotCompared: Not compared (only one side has a result)
regression.bucketNotComparedWhy: Only one side has a result for these cases, so whether they regressed was not measured this time — that is not “unchanged”. Folding them into Unchanged would let a run that aborted halfway report “0 regressed”.
regression.bucketRegressedWhy: This is what the whole report is for: these passed in the baseline run and fail now — they are what this change broke.
regression.bucketUnchangedWhy: The deterministic verdict is the same in both runs (including cases that failed both times). This block excludes “not compared” and “judge drift” — those two have their own blocks above.
regression.caseQuestionBlank: . Whitespace-only questions (including full-width spaces) are rejected, so a case that fails on every replay never gets stored.
regression.contextTurnsSentHint: (= the number of preceding turns the case itself stores; only the user half is replayed. 0 means the case is a single-turn case. If the replay cannot reattach to the same chatroom the whole run aborts — it never silently sends fewer turns.)
regression.driftAvailableNow: Not scored last time, scored now
regression.driftUnavailableNow: Scored last time, not scored now
regression.effectiveBaselineMissing: The baseline run did not record what it actually used, so “where do the two runs differ” cannot be answered this time — do not read the table below as “the two runs used the same settings”.
regression.effectiveDiffCountSuffix: setting(s) differ — at 0 the two runs used the same configuration, so a regression was not caused by the settings.
regression.effectiveIntro: This is the configuration that was actually sent to the answering engine, recorded when the run started — not a fresh read of the profile (if the profile has changed since, this still shows what really ran). Rows marked “From the profile” took whatever the profile under test had at that moment; rows marked “Set for this run” are the ones deliberately changed.
regression.effectiveRestHint: This table only lists the settings that “Run this suite” can change. The rest of the profile (content policy, output rules, direct QA answers, tag filtering…) always comes from the profile — that endpoint structurally cannot touch them, and sending one is rejected as an unknown override field.
regression.exportColumns: Seven columns: case / expectation / actual answer / pass or fail / cited documents / judge score / why it failed. “Pass or fail” is literally one of two words, with the failure detail in its own column (in a downstream pivot table every distinct detail sentence stuffed into a status column becomes a new status value); “cited documents” lists the documents actually cited, writes “(no hits)” when there were none and states the total when the list is capped — a blank cell would read as “this question hit nothing”.
regression.exportPartialHint: Aborted or still-running executions can be exported too, but the CSV only contains the cases that finished — its last row states how many rows there are and why the run stopped. Do not read it as “the whole suite ran”.
regression.exportPartialPrefix: This execution was aborted; the exported CSV only contains
regression.exportPartialSuffix: case results, and its last row states the row count and the abort reason — do not read it as “the whole suite ran”.
regression.fromLog: Create case from a Q&A record
regression.fromLogContextCost: Off by default. Every preceding turn is a real Q&A on every execution (one chatbot call, one Q&A quota unit). Exceeding the limit rejects the whole request instead of keeping only the most recent turns — truncation would produce a case that looks complete but lost its earliest context.
regression.fromLogIncludeContextOn: Follow this record’s preceding-turn chain and carry the whole conversation into the case
regression.fromLogIntro: The question, the preceding turns and the assertions are all derived by the backend from that record: if it had hits, the expectation is “still cites the same primary source”; if it had none, “still honestly answers not found”. When nothing can be derived, no empty-assertion case is created.
regression.fromLogNeedsHistory: A positive integer; it is the conversation id shown on each row of the History page. Besides the settings permission, this endpoint also requires the “Q&A history” capability — it reads questions, answers and source document names.
regression.fromLogRefuse: Two kinds of “cannot derive” must be read differently: this record is unsuitable (no answer, blocked by policy, too many preceding turns) — pick another record or create the case manually; or the upstream data is broken (unexpected hit-list shape, first hit has no document identity) — that is not something you did wrong, please report it.
regression.hitsWhy: Each block below gains two columns, “Cited in baseline” and “Cited in this run”: the most common cause of a regression is “it used to cite A and now cites B”, and that is only visible with both sides next to each other. Every stored hit keeps the document identity and where it came from, never the full text, and there is a per-case cap — when the list is capped the cell states the real total, so do not read it as “only these documents were cited”.
regression.intro: A suite is a set of questions that carry their own assertions. One execution replays the whole suite, judges each case pass or fail, and compares the result against a previous run — the regressed ones are exactly what this change broke.
regression.judgeAvgBasePrefix: The subjective average covers only the
regression.judgeAvgBaseSuffix: could not be judged and were not counted as 0, which would have dragged the average down. Cases without a judge score:
regression.judgeNoThreshold: The subjective score never affects pass/fail and has no threshold: a low score does not turn a case red. Only “has criteria but was not scored” is flagged as not judged.
regression.limitContextTurnsWhy: . Every turn costs one Q&A quota unit on every execution.
regression.limitsWhy: Anything over a limit is rejected outright; the first few cases are never run on their own — that would be a report that looks all green. Split large suites into several suites.

serviceKey.ackOnce: I understand the secret is shown only once, and I have its destination ready.
serviceKey.intro: Machine credentials are for callers that are not people — today only the nightly data health scan. A credential is not a platform master key: each one carries a single scope, endpoints outside that scope always refuse it, and on any endpoint that expects a signed-in identity it does not constitute an identity at all. Issuing and revoking require a platform administrator; auditors can read the inventory.
serviceKey.issueBeforeWarn: Once you press issue, the secret is shown this one time. The system keeps only its SHA-256 hash, so closing this page, reloading it, or pressing “I have saved it” puts the secret out of reach for good — there is no “show it again”, only revoke and re-issue. Have its destination ready before you press issue.
serviceKey.issueDestinationHint: In production the destination is the product-health-scan-key secret in Secret Manager: copy it with the button below and paste it there. Do not print the secret in a terminal — that leaves it in shell history, in the argument list visible to ps, and in any screen recording.
serviceKey.listStoredHint: This table can never return a secret: the system keeps only the SHA-256 hash plus the last four characters for identification. If you cannot tell which credential a row is, go by the name and those four characters; if they still do not match anything, revoke it and issue a new one rather than guessing.
serviceKey.name: What it is for
serviceKey.nameHint: During rotation you have to be able to tell which row belongs to which consumer, so name the consumer (for example “nightly health-scan CronJob”). The name grants nothing; it only decides whether this table still makes sense to you later.
serviceKey.none: There are no valid machine credentials. The schedule needs one to run — without it the job fails every day, and that failure is written only into the job’s log.
serviceKey.plainOnce: This is the only time this credential’s secret is shown. Leave or reload this page and all that is left on screen are the last four characters; the system itself holds only the hash, so nobody can read it back.
serviceKey.revokeHint: Revoking is a soft delete and takes effect immediately (unlike a sign-in session, which waits out its lifetime): the row stays, because “this credential existed, and who revoked it when” is a fact auditing has to be able to look up — and while the row is there that secret can never be brought back. “Include revoked” above is ticked by default, so revoked credentials are listed too; untick it to see only the ones still in use.
serviceKey.rotateHint: Zero-downtime rotation: issue the new credential first (one scope may hold several valid credentials at once), put it into Secret Manager and let the consumer pick it up, then watch “last used” — when the old one stops advancing, nobody is using it any more, and only then do you revoke it. Forcing one credential per scope would leave a gap in the middle of every rotation during which the schedule is mute and nobody notices.
serviceKey.scopeHint: The scope decides which endpoints this credential may call, compared for exact equality — a value outside the list is refused at issue time. The available scopes and what each one covers are in the table below.
serviceKey.scopesHint: This table is the endpoint’s own value set, not a copy kept by this page. A scope decides what a credential may do, rather than merely whether one was presented — a health-scan credential is refused on the tenant list, the audit log, timezone writes and on issuing another credential.

settings.gapClassifyLimitReached: The per-request classification limit has been reached: the distinct questions beyond it were not sent for classification this time and are listed as they are under “not sent for classification” below. settings.gapDimensionHint: Picking a dimension is what sends each question off to be classified (once per question, results cached). Without grouping no model is called at all and every question lands in “not sent for classification”.
settings.gapKindOutOfScopeHint: The classifier confidently decided these questions do not fall under any code (mostly greetings and small talk). Either widen the vocabulary, or use “Exclude” on each row to take them out.
settings.gapKindUnclassifiedHint: These questions were never sent for classification: either no grouping dimension was given, or they fell outside the per-request classification limit (the budget is spent on the most-asked questions). This is a boundary of the report, not a property of the data.
settings.gapKindUndeterminedHint: The classifier ran but reached no conclusion — this covers both “the model said it was unsure” and “the classifier is broken across the board”, which cannot be told apart at the type level, so this report does not pretend to tell them apart either. When this row is unusually large, go read the backend error log — it does not mean “these questions are all small talk”.
settings.glossaryApplyAgentHint: Unchecked tables are reachable only through skills; the main agent cannot query them. Their “when to consult” text also disappears from the main agent's tool list — that text was a routing signal, so make sure the corresponding skill's description can take over, otherwise the main agent may not even call the skill.

settings.glossaryMgmtIntro: A glossary lets the QA agent look up definitions of domain terms; “When to consult” is the tool description the LLM uses to decide when to query this table. Aliases now live in Alias tables, and each conversation profile decides whether glossary lookup applies them.
settings.glossaryNormalizeRegexPlacehold: e.g. [-.\s] to strip separators; no quantifiers (* + ? {})
settings.glossaryRegexFormatHint: ; must be a valid regex, with no quantifiers (* + ? {}) and at most one alternation
settings.groundingScoreFloorNote: This field cannot be left blank (default 0.5). It is not a pre-check ticket — when the top retrieval score falls below it, the turn is answered as an honest no-answer without asking the LLM at all, and the sources are cleared too. The scale depends on the reranker in use (weaviate 0–1, llm_reranker 1–5, jina 0–1, bge_reranker can be negative), so this number must be recalibrated whenever the reranker changes — otherwise the same 0.5 may block nothing at all, or block every single question. Deliberately unlike the “QA direct answer” field, which may be left blank.
settings.groupMgmtIntro: Groups are permission groups: capabilities are defined on the group, and a user inherits them by joining (the union across all their groups). Datasets belong to a group, and write access follows group membership.

settings.outputRuleConstNameHint: The prompt has to carry a placeholder of the same name (no surrounding spaces, no braces in the name itself), for example
settings.outputRuleConstantRouteDesc: The prompt only carries a placeholder; this rule fills in the actual value from the intent decision made for this turn, and falls back to the default value when no case holds.
settings.outputRuleFlagConflictDesc: When a topic has several equally current records, a separate paragraph is added after the answer listing each one’s as-of date and source name, and saying that these may not agree — rather than picking one. That paragraph cannot say what each one claims: output processing runs without AI and has only the dates and source names, so summarizing what those records say would be a statement with nothing behind it. One document split into several chunks counts once; if fewer than two sources have a readable date and name, the paragraph is not added.
settings.outputRuleLinkAnchorDesc: Turns bare URLs, angle-bracket URLs and HTML anchor tags into markdown links [text](url). Answers are rendered as markdown, so an HTML anchor tag left in place shows up on screen as a literal tag.
settings.outputRuleLinkHideUrlDesc: When the visible text is exactly the URL, replaces it with the host plus the last path segment; the URL itself stays as the link target.
settings.outputRuleLinkMaxDesc: Beyond the cap, keeps the first few links and leaves only the visible text of the rest.
settings.outputRuleListMarkerDesc: Rewrites line-leading 1), (1) and 一、 into 1., keeping the original number and indentation (no renumbering).
settings.outputRuleMaxBulletsDesc: Beyond the cap, only reports a violation; it does not drop any bullet.
settings.outputRuleMaxCharsDesc: Beyond the cap, only reports a violation and never truncates the answer — cutting at a sentence boundary drops the proviso that makes the answer correct. The cap can be overridden per code of this turn’s intent decision.
settings.outputRuleStateAsOfDesc: When the data an answer cites carries an as-of date, a note like “(this information is as of 2024-11-30)” is appended to the closing sentence. With several cited records the oldest one wins — once a passage cites an older record it only holds good up to that day, and printing the most recent date would vouch for the part that has already gone stale. The note joins the end of the last prose line; if that line is a table, list, quote, heading or code fence it starts its own paragraph instead of being swallowed by it.
settings.outputRuleStripBracketTagDesc: Removes bracketed tags at the start of a line. The list below says which ones; brackets outside the list are kept as they are.
settings.outputRuleStripHeadingDesc: Removes markdown heading lines and bold mini-heading opening lines; when such a line still carries content, only the marker goes, not the whole line.
settings.outputRuleStripLeadPhraseDesc: Removes boilerplate at the start of the answer. The list below says which ones; when several match, the longest one wins.
settings.outputRuleStripLeadYesnoDesc: Removes a standalone “Yes.” / “No.” sentence at the start of the answer; only a whole sentence goes, never half of one.
settings.outputRuleValuesHintSuffix: characters; leading and trailing spaces are stripped.
settings.outputRulesIntro: Deterministic post-processing (no AI) applied to the whole answer after it is generated and before it reaches the compliance gate. The order of the three output stages is fixed by the platform and cannot be changed.
settings.outputRulesMaxHint: A profile holds only so many rules; once the cap is reached “Add rule” is disabled — delete one to make room.
settings.outputRulesStreamingCostOff: No output rule is enabled, so answers still appear word by word. Enabling any single rule switches this profile to showing the whole answer at once when generation finishes, with nothing in between (a rule can only judge the answer as a whole).
settings.outputRulesStreamingCostOn: Output rules are on: answers for this profile no longer appear word by word. A rule can only judge the answer as a whole (total links, list numbering, length), so the answer appears all at once when generation finishes, with nothing shown in between. Disable every rule to get word-by-word output back.

settings.qaDirectIntro: When a question exactly matches a QA set’s question, return that answer verbatim without AI rephrasing; judge mode adds one LLM decision.
settings.qaDirectScoreFloorDep: Empty = not calibrated: with adjudication on it means no pre-filtering and everything goes to the judge; with adjudication off it means only the “normalized exact match” layer is used, which is a safe setup. But when the mode is “exact match” and reranking is off on the “Generation” tab, a floor must not be set — only the raw retrieval score is left and that is not a calibratable scale, so saving is rejected. Two ways out: turn reranking on (the score then comes from the reranker), or leave this empty.
settings.reasoningGroupIntentDesc: Analyzes the language, keywords, time range, and filename intent of the user’s input (the intent-detection stage of traditional search mode).
settings.reasoningGroupJudgeDesc: Judges whether retrieved material is sufficient to answer (the answerability grounding gate and tiered-retrieval IsAnswerable), QA direct-answer adjudication, and content-policy topic adjudication.
settings.reasoningGroupRecommendDesc: The follow-up question suggestions and the chat-room title produced after each answer. This group runs every round (suggested questions are on by default), making it the only one of the five that costs money on every turn — pointing it at a smaller model has the most impact.
settings.reasoningGroupSkillDesc: The tool loop and reply inside a tenant’s custom skill (a skill’s output is a tool result fed back to the main agent).
settings.reasoningGroupToolsDesc: In agent chat mode, the reasoning for choosing and calling tools each round (excludes final answer generation).
settings.reasoningGroupsIntro: Each internal LLM call other than the main answer (what the user finally sees) can use its own model and reasoning depth. Leave empty to inherit the main model / minimal thinking.
settings.recencyWindowNote: The “recent data window” is not a switch that takes effect on its own: it only appears when intent classification decides the question is asking for the latest data, and when the classification is inconclusive the whole condition is discarded together with the window. The reason is that the window is the only predicate with no “untagged” branch — keeping it would filter out documents that have no publication date at all.
settings.rerankerScaleNote: Each reranker uses a different score scale, so switching reranker means recalibrating the score floor on the “QA direct answer” tab and the one on the answerability gate. Current scale:
settings.scoreFloorRange: 0 or greater; no upper bound (each reranker uses its own scale)
settings.scoreScaleRecalibrate: The score scale just changed (you changed the reranker model, the rerank switch, or the data source ratio). This floor was calibrated against the old scale — recalibrate it: a number from a 1–5 scale moved onto a 0–1 scale becomes a condition that never blocks anything.
settings.skillAllowedToolsHint: Only the checked tools can be used by this skill; anything unchecked simply does not exist at run time — it is not “disallowed”, it is unreachable.
settings.skillDescriptionHint: Describe both what this skill does and when it should be used — this is the only thing the agent uses to decide whether to call it, so a vague description means it never triggers.
settings.skillInputSchemaHint: A JSON Schema describing what the agent must pass when calling this tool (top level must be an object; document_ids, indexes and dsl are not allowed). Leave empty and the agent calls it with a single natural-language task.
settings.skillInputSchemaLenSuffix: characters: this schema is appended verbatim after the “what it does” description to form the tool description, and it enters the system prompt on every turn. Because what is measured is not the number of characters in this box, this field has no input length limit; if you go over, the save result tells you.
settings.skillInstructionsHint: Loaded only when the skill is called, as its system prompt. If the steps must run in order, spell them out here.
settings.skillMaxIterationsHintPrefix: How many rounds this skill’s inner loop may run (
settings.skillMaxIterationsHintSuffix: ). Too low and it gets cut off before finishing.
settings.skillMgmtIntro: A skill is a reusable capability pack: instructions plus a set of tools. The agent decides on its own when to call it, based on “what it does”. Agent mode only.
settings.skillNameHintSuffix: characters; cannot start or end with a hyphen, and no consecutive hyphens. This is also the tool name the agent sees.
settings.skillNestedHintPrefix: Referenced skills become tools this skill can call. Cycles are not allowed; nesting depth is capped at
settings.supportContactHint: Shown on the login page, where anyone can see it; leave it empty to hide it
settings.tagCodeHint: Codes go verbatim into the retrieval condition, so they must not contain , ' " \ * ? (those get rewritten or cut somewhere along “import matching → DSL string → upstream matching”). Two codes differing only in case or full/half width cannot coexist either — the matcher cannot tell them apart, while retrieval can only send one of the two spellings.
settings.tagCoverageScanHint: “No content found” and “files that cannot be enumerated” do not mean “not tagged” — they mean “not known yet”, so they are listed separately and excluded from the denominator; counting them as tagged would overstate coverage. Coverage is a report on how much is tagged, not the test for whether filtering can be enabled: that is decided by “every document carries this column” — see the retrieval filter section below.
settings.tagDimensionsIntro: A tag dimension declares one physical filter slot as a business dimension and gives it a controlled vocabulary; at query time intent classification picks the codes and compiles them into a retrieval filter. The engine itself knows no business codes — it only knows “this field equals this string”.
settings.tagFilterBlockedHint: This table has nothing to do with a dimension’s kind: “unset” is now a sentinel value written at import time and all three kinds can express it, so how much is tagged does not affect whether documents get dropped. The only remaining gap is “this file does not have the column at all” — that is a structural fact, and only re-importing (or importing row by row) fixes it.
settings.tagFilterBlockedTitle: The dimensions below are not carried by every document yet; turning filtering on now would silently exclude those files
settings.tagFilterCoverageWarnBlocked: Some files have not written this column into the index (the dimension did not exist when they were imported, or they were imported as a folder). Turning filtering on in this state silently excludes those files — the filter matches “this column equals a code or equals unset”, and those files do not have the column at all. Agent mode has no no-result relaxation ladder, so a filtered-out document is really gone and users just experience it as “some data cannot be found”. That is exactly why this switch is off by default.
settings.tagFilterCoverageWarnOk: Every document currently carries this column, so filtering can be turned on. Empty cells were written as “Unset” at import time and the filter matches them too, so how much is tagged does not affect whether documents get dropped. Only one thing to watch from here: a folder import never has field slots, so importing a new batch that way loses the column again — switch that batch to a row-by-row import to bring it back.
settings.tagFilterFixNotMapped: Re-importing once adds the column, and empty cells are filled in with “Unset” automatically.
settings.tagFilterFixWholeFile: A folder import has no field slot to carry this column: either re-import that batch row by row, or do not filter on this dimension.
settings.tagFilterIntro: Once enabled, a question is first classified into business dimensions and the result is compiled into a retrieval filter for the engine. When the classification is inconclusive the whole condition is discarded (the recency window with it) — it never degrades into a looser condition.
settings.tagFilterNotMapped: The dimension did not exist at import time, so that column never reached the index
settings.tagFilterWholeFile: Imported as a folder — the whole file is one document, so there are no field slots
settings.tagKindHint: Single = one of several; multi = several at once; date = compared by magnitude. Date slots (date2/date3) can only be the date type, and no other slot can be — a mismatched pair is rejected upstream on every single search.
settings.tagRoleHint: Roles are what the engine’s built-in mechanisms look for: valid_until/as_of only on date dimensions, fact_topic/superseded_by only on single-value dimensions. A mismatch raises no error — the mechanism simply skips this dimension, so the settings page looks fine while that mechanism never took effect at all.
settings.tagSlotHintPrefix: Only the slots product declares to the retrieval engine as custom filter fields (
settings.tagSlotHintSuffix: ) can carry a dimension; DSL references to built-in slots are rejected upstream. One slot can hold only one dimension, and one role can be assigned to only one dimension.
settings.tagVocabularyIntro: The vocabulary is this dimension’s legal value range: on import the column only accepts codes from the list, and intent classification only picks from the same list. For a single/multi dimension whose vocabulary is empty, import rejects every non-empty value in that column.
settings.timeRangeLimitMid: days, and the start time cannot be earlier than
settings.timeRangeLimitPrefix: The time range spans at most
settings.timeRangeLimitSuffix: days ago; a range beyond that is rejected on submit.
